hints: Look closely at what was changed: just one amino acid was swapped for a lab-made one. Think about what one different R-group can do to the folding and 3D shape of the whole protein.

Remember how a protein-digesting enzyme works: the protein to be digested is its substrate, so it must fit into the active site for hydrolysis to happen. Think about both lock-and-key complementarity and induced fit.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the change does**

Think of the antimicrobial protein as the substrate for the protein-digesting enzyme.

Swapping one natural amino acid for a synthetic one changes R-groups, hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds, so the folding and tertiary structure can change.

**Link shape to enzyme action**

For digestion to happen, the protein must fit into the enzyme active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.

In the lock-and-key idea this needs a complementary shape. In the induced fit idea the substrate must be able to trigger the active site to mould around it.

**Check statements 1, 2 and 3**

Statement 1 is sensible, a different amino acid sequence often gives a different tertiary structure.

If the shape is changed, statement 2 follows: it is no longer complementary to the active site. Statement 3 also follows: it cannot induce the correct fit. All three explain why no breakdown occurs, so the answer is A.

options.A: All three statements are valid. A changed tertiary structure (1) leads to loss of complementarity (2) and failure of induced fit (3), so no enzyme-substrate complex forms.
options.B: This misses out statement 3, but induced fit is also part of modern enzyme action, so a failure to induce a fit is also a correct explanation.
options.C: This misses out statement 1, but changing an amino acid can alter bonding and folding, so a different tertiary structure is also a correct explanation.
options.D: This only accepts statement 2. Both the altered tertiary structure and the failure of induced fit are also linked explanations, so D is incomplete.
